To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
feature binding and feature processing engage specific neural resources, regardless of the number of objects and features to be remembered.

(1) feature binding in WM is associated with a specific set of neural regions; and (2) these regions are located in the parietal and temporal cortices, but not in the medial temporal lobar regions or prefrontal cortex.
feature binding in working (temporary) memory involves additional cortical regions beyond those required to maintain individual features.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of visual memory for objects and their constituent features.
the neural correlates of feature binding in visual working (temporary) memory.

the nature of the neural mechanisms that underlie the representation of complex objects in WM and the processes involved in the formation and maintenance of integrated object representations in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
feature binding in WM involves the same neural generators as are involved in the processing of individual features.
binding is supported by the same regions that are active when processing single features but that binding-specific regions are also involved in binding.
the neural correlates of feature binding in visual WM are not limited to a single area, and that they are distributed over several regions of the cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
feature bindings are represented in a distributed manner in the parietal and temporal cortices.
the binding of shape and color features in visual WM is supported by an extended network of regions, including the parietal lobe, lateral and medial temporal lobes, and occipital lobe.
the neural mechanisms of feature binding in WM are different from those of single feature processing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural systems supporting the encoding and temporary retention of feature bindings are distinct from those supporting the temporary retention of individual features.
the neural mechanisms that support feature binding are not identical to those that support the retention of individual features.
feature bindings are not merely an epiphenomenon of feature processing but rather a function of the visual system with specific neural generators.
